systems.name: Cardiovascular system
systems.summary: The heart and blood vessels move blood to deliver oxygen and nutrients and remove wastes.
fields: Right side: body to lungs (pulmonary circuit). Left side: lungs to body (systemic circuit).
Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume.

systems.name: Respiratory system
systems.summary: Brings oxygen in and removes carbon dioxide.
fields: Nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs with about 300 million alveoli.
Occurs across the thin alveolar-capillary membrane by diffusion.
The diaphragm contracts to expand the chest and draw air in.

systems.name: Digestive system
systems.summary: Breaks down food and absorbs nutrients.
fields: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum.
Liver (bile, metabolism), gallbladder, pancreas (enzymes and insulin).
Most absorption happens in the small intestine via villi.

systems.name: Nervous system
fields: Central (brain, spinal cord) and peripheral (nerves). The peripheral part includes somatic and autonomic branches.
Sympathetic ('fight or flight') and parasympathetic ('rest and digest').

systems.name: Endocrine system
systems.summary: Hormones carry slower, longer-lasting signals through the blood.
fields: Pituitary, thyroid, parathyroids, adrenals, pancreas, gonads, pineal.
Most hormone systems use negative feedback, such as thyroid hormone controlled by the hypothalamus and pituitary.

systems.name: Renal and urinary system
systems.summary: Filters blood, balances fluids and electrolytes, regulates blood pressure.
fields: Glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption and secretion, then excretion.
ADH, aldosterone and renin-angiotensin signalling fine-tune water and salt.

systems.name: Musculoskeletal system
systems.summary: Support, movement, protection and blood cell production.
fields: The adult skeleton has 206 bones. Red marrow makes blood cells.
Skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle. Skeletal muscle contracts by sliding actin and myosin filaments.

systems.name: Immune system
systems.summary: Defends against pathogens and abnormal cells.
fields: Fast, non-specific: barriers, neutrophils, macrophages, complement.
Slower, specific and with memory: T cells and B cells (antibodies).
Train adaptive immunity without causing the disease.

pathology.name: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
pathology.summary: An autoimmune disease in which the immune system destroys insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells.
fields: Loss of beta cells leads to little or no insulin, so cells cannot take up glucose and blood glucose rises.
Type 2 diabetes mainly involves insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency.
Replacing insulin and monitoring glucose are the cornerstones, managed by clinicians.

pathology.name: Hypertension
fields: Often multifactorial: vessel resistance, kidney salt handling, hormonal systems and genetics.
Over years it damages arteries, heart, brain and kidneys and raises the risk of stroke and heart attack.
Often has no symptoms, which is why measurement matters.

pathology.name: Asthma
pathology.summary: A chronic inflammatory airway disease with reversible airflow obstruction.
fields: Airway inflammation, smooth-muscle constriction and mucus narrow the airways in response to triggers.
Wheeze, cough and breathlessness that vary over time.

pathology.name: Myocardial infarction
pathology.summary: Death of heart muscle caused by blocked blood supply.
fields: Usually rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque in a coronary artery forms a clot that blocks flow.
Without oxygen, cardiomyocytes die within hours, so speed of treatment matters.
Anyone with chest pain or suspected heart attack should seek emergency care immediately.

pathology.name: Sickle cell disease
pathology.summary: An inherited blood disorder caused by a mutation in the beta-globin gene.
fields: Glu6Val substitution makes haemoglobin S polymerise when deoxygenated, bending red cells into sickle shapes.
Cells block small vessels and break down early, causing pain episodes and anaemia.
Autosomal recessive: carriers have one copy (sickle cell trait).

pathology.name: Alzheimer's disease
pathology.summary: The most common cause of dementia, a progressive neurodegenerative disease.
fields: Extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular tau tangles, with synapse and neuron loss.
Often begins in medial temporal lobe circuits, affecting recent memory first.
The causes are multifactorial and still being researched.

molecular.name: DNA structure
molecular.summary: A double helix of two antiparallel strands.
fields: Nucleotides: a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate and a base (A, T, G or C).
A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds); G pairs with C (three).
Use the DNA Toolkit button to transcribe and translate a sequence.

molecular.name: Central dogma
molecular.summary: DNA is transcribed into RNA, and RNA is translated into protein.
fields: RNA polymerase copies a gene into mRNA in the nucleus.
Ribosomes read mRNA codons and tRNAs deliver amino acids.
Reverse transcription (retroviruses) and RNA that is never translated (e.g. tRNA, rRNA) show the picture is richer.

molecular.name: Proteins
molecular.summary: Chains of amino acids folded into functional 3D shapes.
fields: Primary (sequence), secondary (helices, sheets), tertiary (3D fold), quaternary (multiple chains).
Enzymes, receptors, transporters, structural fibres and antibodies.
Misfolded proteins are implicated in several diseases.

molecular.name: Enzymes
molecular.summary: Biological catalysts that speed up reactions.
fields: Lower activation energy by binding the substrate at the active site.
Competitive inhibitors compete for the active site; non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere.
Activity depends on temperature and pH.

molecular.name: Cell membrane
molecular.summary: A phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins.
fields: Small non-polar molecules cross easily; ions and large polar molecules need channels or transporters.
Passive (diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion) and active (pumps such as Na+/K+-ATPase).

molecular.name: Cellular energy: ATP
molecular.summary: ATP is the cell's main short-term energy currency.
fields: Glycolysis (cytoplasm), then the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria.
Aerobic respiration makes far more ATP per glucose than glycolysis alone (textbook estimates are around 30 ATP).

frontiers.name: mRNA vaccines
frontiers.summary: Vaccines that deliver mRNA instructions so cells make a harmless antigen.
fields: ESTABLISHED technology: authorised and used at large scale from 2020.
Researchers are studying the same platform for other infections and for cancer vaccines. Results so far are early.

frontiers.name: CRISPR gene editing
frontiers.summary: Programmable nucleases (such as Cas9) that cut DNA at chosen sites.
fields: ESTABLISHED as a research tool. Casgevy, a CRISPR-based therapy for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassaemia, was approved in the UK and US in late 2023.
Base editing, prime editing and in-body delivery. Safety and cost remain active questions.

frontiers.name: GLP-1 receptor agonists
frontiers.summary: Drugs that mimic the gut hormone GLP-1.
fields: ESTABLISHED for type 2 diabetes and obesity treatment under medical supervision.
Possible effects on other conditions are being studied. Long-term data are still accumulating.

frontiers.name: AI protein structure prediction
frontiers.summary: Deep-learning systems such as AlphaFold predict protein 3D structures from sequence.
fields: ESTABLISHED as a widely used research tool. The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognised work on computational protein design and structure prediction.
Predictions are models and still need experimental validation.

frontiers.name: CAR-T cell therapy
frontiers.summary: A patient's T cells are engineered to recognise cancer cells.
fields: Applying it to solid tumours and autoimmune disease is under active investigation.

frontiers.name: The gut microbiome
frontiers.summary: Trillions of microbes in the gut interact with metabolism, immunity and possibly the brain.
fields: EMERGING field. Strong evidence for some uses (e.g. faecal transplant for recurrent C. difficile infection), but many claims about other conditions are still preliminary.
Illustrates the difference between correlation and causation.

chronicles.q: FICTIONAL SCENARIO. A 25-year-old fictional patient, 'Alex', runs a marathon on a hot day, drinks only plain water for hours and develops confusion. Blood tests show a very low sodium concentration. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Hyponatraemia from excess water intake and sodium loss
chronicles.explanation: Sweating loses sodium; replacing large volumes with plain water dilutes remaining sodium (exercise-associated hyponatraemia). Low sodium can cause brain swelling and confusion.

chronicles.q: FICTIONAL SCENARIO. 'Sam', a fictional 8-year-old, has a wheeze that worsens during exercise and in cold air, and improves with a bronchodilator. Which process best explains the wheeze?
options: Narrowing of the airways from smooth-muscle constriction and inflammation
chronicles.explanation: In asthma, inflamed hypersensitive airways constrict, reducing airflow and producing wheeze. Bronchodilators relax airway smooth muscle.

chronicles.q: FICTIONAL SCENARIO. A fictional patient has weight loss, excessive thirst, frequent urination and a very high blood glucose. Which hormone is deficient or ineffective in the underlying disease?
chronicles.explanation: Without effective insulin action, glucose stays in the blood. Once it exceeds the kidney's reabsorption capacity, it pulls water into the urine (osmotic diuresis), causing thirst and polyuria.

chronicles.q: FICTIONAL SCENARIO. After a stroke, a fictional patient understands speech well but speaks in slow, effortful, short phrases. Which area is most likely damaged?
chronicles.explanation: Non-fluent (Broca's) aphasia involves impaired speech production with relatively preserved comprehension.

chronicles.q: FICTIONAL SCENARIO. A fictional patient has swelling of both ankles, breathlessness when lying flat and crackles at the base of both lungs. Which is the most likely underlying mechanism?
options: The heart is not pumping effectively, so fluid backs up into the lungs and tissues
Excess red blood cell production only
Complete failure of the digestive tract
chronicles.explanation: Heart failure raises venous and pulmonary pressures, pushing fluid out of capillaries into lungs (pulmonary oedema) and dependent tissues.

chronicles.q: FICTIONAL SCENARIO. A fictional patient has chronic fatigue and pallor. Blood tests show small (microcytic) red blood cells and low ferritin. What is the most likely diagnosis category?
chronicles.explanation: Iron is needed for haemoglobin synthesis. Low ferritin shows depleted iron stores, producing small pale red cells. B12 deficiency typically gives large (macrocytic) cells.

chronicles.q: FICTIONAL SCENARIO. A fictional patient takes a drug that blocks the enzyme converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II (an ACE inhibitor). Which change in physiology is expected?
options: Lower blood pressure through reduced vasoconstriction and aldosterone
Higher blood pressure through increased vasoconstriction
Increased heart rate and cardiac contractility directly
chronicles.explanation: Angiotensin II is a vasoconstrictor and stimulates aldosterone. Blocking its formation relaxes vessels and reduces salt and water retention.
